summary: Specifies the IPv6 Flow Label field and the minimum requirements for nodes that label flows, forward labeled packets, and set up flow state. The label lets devices classify flows using only fixed-position fields in the main header. It replaces RFC 3697 and updates RFC 2205 and RFC 2460.

eli5.summary: Packets of one conversation can wear the same colored sticker. Then a router can group them at a glance, without reading further inside. This sets the rules for the sticker.

subtitle: How hosts and routers should set and treat the 20-bit IPv6 Flow Label so flows can be classified from fixed header fields.

tldr.problem: Classifying a flow normally needs the 5-tuple, but ports may be hidden by fragmentation or encryption or sit behind a chain of extension headers, which is slow to walk.
tldr.mechanism: Source nodes label each flow with a 20-bit Flow Label drawn from an approximation to a uniform distribution, and the label is combined with the source and destination addresses to identify the flow. Forwarding nodes must not change a non-zero label, apart from compelling security reasons.
tldr.outcome: Routers can classify flows and spread load, for example across ECMP or LAG paths, using only fixed-position header fields. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3697 and updates RFC 2205 and RFC 2460.

facts.label: Flow identifier
facts.value: Flow Label + Source Address + Destination Address

today: RFC 6437 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 3697 and updates RFC 2205 and RFC 2460.

sections.title: Why Label Flows
sections.content:
At the network layer, a flow is a sequence of packets from one source to one unicast, anycast or multicast destination that a node chooses to label as a flow. It is not necessarily a one-to-one match with a transport connection.

Flow classifiers have traditionally used the 5-tuple: source address, destination address, source port, destination port and transport protocol. Some of these may be unavailable because of fragmentation or encryption, or may be inefficient to find past a chain of IPv6 extension headers. Using the 3-tuple of Flow Label, Source Address and Destination Address allows efficient classification from IPv6 main header fields in fixed positions. It also makes it easier to introduce new transport protocols later.

The label can be used in stateless scenarios, where no node stores flow information, and stateful ones, where nodes keep state and may use signaling such as RSVP or GIST. This document concentrates on the stateless model as the default mechanism. A specific goal is to encourage the label for stateless load distribution across Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) and Link Aggregation Group (LAG) paths. It replaces RFC 3697 and Section 6 and Appendix A of RFC 2460, with the rationale in RFC 6436.
sections.eli5: Reading every detail on a parcel to sort it is slow. A sticker in the same spot on every parcel of one order lets the sorter group them in a glance.

sections.title: The Flow Label Field
sections.content:
The Flow Label is a 20-bit field in the IPv6 header. A value of zero means the packet has not been labeled. Classifiers use the triplet of Flow Label, Source Address and Destination Address to identify the flow. How flows are treated and how flow state is established are out of scope.

Label values should vary a lot in their bits so they work as input to a hash for load distribution, and third parties should be unlikely to guess the next value. A discrete uniform distribution has both properties, so an approximation to it is preferable. The RFC deliberately sets no precise mathematical requirements.

Once non-zero, the label is expected to arrive unchanged. A forwarding node MUST either leave a non-zero label unchanged or change it only for compelling operational security reasons (Section 6.1). Because nobody can verify that a label was left alone or is uniformly distributed, forwarding nodes such as routers and load distributors MUST NOT depend only on labels being uniformly distributed. If used as a hash key, the label bits MUST be combined with bits from other places in the packet, typically parts of the usual 5-tuple, so load distribution still works even if labels are poorly distributed.

Packet flows should not be reordered, and a label of zero does not imply that reordering is acceptable.
sections.eli5: A zero sticker means no sticker. Once a real sticker is on, nobody should peel it off. Because anyone might have changed it, sorters should also look at other clues.

sections.title: Labeling in the Stateless Scenario
sections.content:
Source nodes SHOULD assign each unrelated transport connection and application data stream to a new flow. A typical definition is any set of packets with the same 5-tuple, which a source always has convenient access to. It is RECOMMENDED that source hosts set the same label on every packet of a flow, chosen from an approximation to a discrete uniform distribution. The algorithm is not mandated, but it SHOULD give values that are unique with high probability. If two simultaneous flows with the same addresses get the same value by chance, they simply get the same treatment, which is harmless if rare.

Two suggested approaches are a 20-bit hash of the 5-tuple values (an example is in the appendix) or a pseudo-random number generator, which needs minimal local state to remember the label for each transport socket. Assigning labels sequentially is NOT RECOMMENDED, since on-path observers could guess the next value. A source that does not otherwise set the label MUST set it to zero.

A forwarding node that sees a zero label MAY change it, and then it is RECOMMENDED to set a uniformly distributed value as sources do. Such a node may lack the full 5-tuple, especially for fragmented packets, so it might use the 5-tuple when possible and the 2-tuple of destination and source address otherwise, or use the 2-tuple always. Setting labels in forwarding nodes could place a considerable per-packet load on first-hop or ingress routers, so it MUST be a configurable option, disabled by default.
sections.eli5: The sender should give each conversation its own random-looking sticker number and use the same one on every packet in it. Counting 1, 2, 3 is a bad idea because others could guess the next one.

sections.title: Flow State Establishment
sections.content:
A node that sets the label MAY also take part in a method that gives specific treatment to specific flows, possibly using signaling. Any such method MUST NOT disturb nodes in the stateless scenario, so a node that sets labels under a stateful scheme MUST choose labels that follow the rules of Section 3. The RFC gives no further detail on stateful methods.

Section 5 makes one essential correction to RFC 2205: RFC 2460 shrank the Flow Label field from 24 to 20 bits, so the references to a 24-bit field in Section A.9 of RFC 2205 are updated.
sections.eli5: If a sender and the network agree on special handling, the sender must still pick stickers by the same ordinary rules, so everyone else is not confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The label is not protected in any way, even when IPsec authentication is used, so an on-path attacker can forge it and any change en route is undetectable. A pseudo-random label cannot readily be guessed, and a hash algorithm SHOULD include a step that makes the value significantly difficult to predict.

Covert channel. Seemingly random labels could carry hidden data. Where the risk matters, the only certain defense is for a firewall to rewrite non-zero labels. Such a firewall SHOULD rewrite them as a forwarding node would for a zero label, and MUST NOT set non-zero labels to zero.

Theft and denial of service. An adversary might get service the network did not intend by changing headers or injecting packets. Networks SHOULD NOT make resource allocation decisions based on flow labels without some external means of assurance. An attacker could set every label reaching a router to one value, or cycle values rapidly, to degrade stateless load distribution or confuse a stateful classifier. Stateless classifiers should not use the label alone, and stateful classifiers should detect and ignore suspect values. The risk is closely tied to address spoofing, and ingress filtering reduces it.

IPsec and tunnels. IPsec does not include the Flow Label in its cryptographic calculations (in tunnel mode, the outer header's label), so changing it cannot break an integrity check, and IPsec gives no defense against modification. The inner header's label must not be changed by decapsulation. The label does not remove the need for packet filtering on headers past the IP header.
sections.eli5: The sticker is not locked, so a mischievous person could swap it. That is why sorters should not trust it alone, and why random numbers are safer than guessable ones.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 3697
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 3697, this specification:

  • encourages non-zero flow label values and clearly defines how to set one;
  • encourages a stateless model with uniformly distributed values;
  • does not specify any details of a stateful model;
  • keeps the rule that the label must not be changed en route, but allows routers to set it on behalf of hosts that do not;
  • discusses the covert channel risk and its consequences for firewalls.

Further detail is in RFC 6436.
sections.eli5: The new rules ask people to actually use the stickers, to keep it simple, and to watch out for sneaky messages hidden in them.

sections.title: An Example 20-Bit Hash
sections.content:
The appendix gives one example of a stateless way to make a label from the 5-tuple, based on a von Neumann algorithm known to give an approximately uniform distribution. The RFC says choosing a suitable hash is not trivial and that extensive practical experience is expected to be needed to find the best choices.

In outline: split the addresses into 64-bit halves, add the source and destination halves and the protocol number with unsigned 64-bit arithmetic, extract 16 bits with the von Neumann method (pairs 01 give 0, pairs 10 give 1, 00 and 11 are discarded), add the two port numbers, shift 4 bits left and mask with 0xfffff. A result of exactly zero is set to 1. The example has no step to prevent predictability, which Section 6 recommends.
sections.eli5: The appendix shows one recipe that mixes up the details of a conversation into a number that looks random.
